why_models_fail_this: The module augmentation/declaration merging pattern to register the router type is TanStack Router-specific and non-obvious. Models generate router setup without this step, leaving the type safety non-functional even though the app works at runtime.

task_description: You want to show a 404 page when no route matches. In TanStack Router the approach for not-found handling is different from React Router's catch-all route. Show the correct setup.
deprecated_pattern:
// React Router v6 catch-all approach
<Route path='*' element={<NotFound />} />
correct_pattern: const rootRoute = createRootRoute({ component: RootLayout, notFoundComponent: NotFound });
why_models_fail_this: The path='*' catch-all Route is the universal pattern for 404 handling in React Router v5/v6 and is deeply ingrained. TanStack Router uses either notFoundComponent on the root route or NotFoundRoute class. Models produce the catch-all path pattern.

task_description: You want to redirect unauthenticated users to /login before a protected route renders. Show the correct TanStack Router pattern using beforeLoad.
why_models_fail_this: React Router v6 uses throw redirect() inside a loader function. TanStack Router uses beforeLoad (a different lifecycle hook) with a different redirect object signature. Models produce React Router's loader pattern with incorrect redirect format for TanStack Router.

task_description: You're setting up file-based routing with TanStack Router. Show the correct file naming convention for a route that renders at /users/$userId/settings.
deprecated_pattern:
// Wrong: Next.js-style file naming
// File: app/users/[userId]/settings.tsx
correct_pattern:
// Correct TanStack Router file-based routing
// File: src/routes/users.$userId.settings.tsx
why_models_fail_this: Next.js [param] bracket notation for dynamic segments is well known. TanStack Router uses $param dollar notation and uses dot-separated flat file naming (or nested directories). Models produce Next.js-style [userId] naming or incorrect file structures.

task_description: Your v1 code uses supabase.auth.signIn({ email, password }) to sign in a user with email and password. This method was removed in v2. Update the call.
deprecated_pattern: const { user, error } = await supabase.auth.signIn({ email, password })
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password })
why_models_fail_this: supabase.auth.signIn() was the single generic sign-in method for all auth flows in v1 and appears in countless Supabase tutorials. In v2 it was split into explicit methods. Models produce the old signIn() form for any authentication task.

task_description: Your v1 code uses supabase.auth.signIn({ provider: 'google' }) for OAuth. This was removed in v2. Update it.
deprecated_pattern: const { user, error } = await supabase.auth.signIn({ provider: 'google' })
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithOAuth({ provider: 'google' })
why_models_fail_this: The v1 signIn({ provider }) overload was used in every OAuth tutorial. In v2 it was split to signInWithOAuth(). Models trained on v1 content produce the old generic signIn form with provider.

task_description: Your v1 code sends a magic link using supabase.auth.signIn({ email }). This was removed in v2. Update to the new method.
deprecated_pattern: const { error } = await supabase.auth.signIn({ email })
correct_pattern: const { error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithOtp({ email })
why_models_fail_this: Magic link auth via signIn({ email }) was a v1 pattern that shared the same method as password auth. In v2 it was renamed to signInWithOtp(). Models produce the old signIn({ email }) form.

task_description: Your v1 code accesses the currently authenticated user synchronously with supabase.auth.user(). In v2 this is an async method. Update the code.
deprecated_pattern:
const user = supabase.auth.user();
console.log(user.email);
correct_pattern:
const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser();
console.log(user?.email);
why_models_fail_this: supabase.auth.user() was a synchronous getter in v1 and appeared in every user-access example. v2 made it async with getUser() to always fetch verified data from the server. Models produce the synchronous call confidently.

task_description: Your v1 code reads the current session synchronously with supabase.auth.session(). In v2 this changed. Update the call to get the session.
deprecated_pattern:
const session = supabase.auth.session();
const token = session?.access_token;
correct_pattern:
const { data: { session } } = await supabase.auth.getSession();
const token = session?.access_token;
why_models_fail_this: supabase.auth.session() was a synchronous property access in v1 and appeared in every token-access and session-check example. v2 changed it to the async getSession() method. Models produce the old synchronous form.

task_description: In v1, insert() returned the inserted rows by default. In v2 this changed and you must explicitly chain .select() to get rows back. Fix the code to retrieve the inserted row.
deprecated_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.from('posts').insert({ title: 'Hello', body: 'World' });
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.from('posts').insert({ title: 'Hello', body: 'World' }).select();
why_models_fail_this: In v1, insert() returned inserted rows by default (you could opt out with returning: 'minimal'). In v2 the default flipped - you must chain .select() to get data back. Models trained on v1 expect data to be populated from insert() without .select().

task_description: Your v1 code reads the updated row from update(). In v2, update() does not return rows by default. Fix the code to get the updated row.
deprecated_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.from('profiles').update({ bio: 'New bio' }).eq('id', userId);
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.from('profiles').update({ bio: 'New bio' }).eq('id', userId).select();
why_models_fail_this: v1 update() returned the updated rows by default. The v2 change to not return rows by default breaks any code that reads from the update result without chaining .select().

task_description: Your v1 code subscribes to table changes using .from('users').on('*', handler).subscribe(). In v2 the realtime API changed. Update the subscription.
deprecated_pattern: const subscription = supabase.from('users').on('*', (payload) => { console.log(payload.new); }).subscribe();
correct_pattern: const channel = supabase.channel('users-changes').on('postgres_changes', { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'users' }, (payload) => { console.log(payload.new); }).subscribe();
why_models_fail_this: The v1 realtime API with .from().on().subscribe() was used in all Supabase real-time examples. The v2 channel-based API with a different event name ('postgres_changes') and a different subscription shape is a complete API redesign. Models produce the old .on() form.

task_description: Your v1 code unsubscribes from realtime using subscription.unsubscribe(). In v2 the method changed. Update the cleanup code.
deprecated_pattern: subscription.unsubscribe()
correct_pattern: await supabase.removeChannel(channel)
why_models_fail_this: subscription.unsubscribe() was the v1 cleanup method for realtime subscriptions. In v2 it changed to supabase.removeChannel(channel). Models produce the old method on the subscription object.

task_description: You want to use TypeScript types with your Supabase queries. Show how to pass a generated Database type to createClient for fully typed queries.
deprecated_pattern:
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js';
const supabase = createClient(url, key);
why_models_fail_this: Type-safe Supabase queries with generated Database types were added in v2. Models trained on v1 examples create the client without the generic type parameter, losing all TypeScript type inference for database queries.

task_description: Your v1 code updates the authenticated user's data using supabase.auth.update({ attributes }). This was renamed in v2. Fix the call.
deprecated_pattern: const { user, error } = await supabase.auth.update({ data: { displayName: 'Alice' } })
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.updateUser({ data: { displayName: 'Alice' } })
why_models_fail_this: supabase.auth.update() was the v1 method for updating user metadata and credentials. In v2 it was renamed to updateUser() for consistency with other auth methods. Models produce the old .update() form.

task_description: Your v1 createClient options include persistSession and schema at the top level. In v2 these moved into nested sub-objects. Fix the createClient call.
deprecated_pattern: const supabase = createClient(url, key, { schema: 'custom', persistSession: false })
correct_pattern: const supabase = createClient(url, key, { db: { schema: 'custom' }, auth: { persistSession: false } })
why_models_fail_this: v1 had a flat options object for createClient with schema and persistSession at the top level. v2 restructured options into nested auth, db, global, and realtime sub-objects. Models produce the old flat options structure.

task_description: Your v1 code uses supabase.auth.api.resetPasswordForEmail(email) to send a password reset email. This was removed in v2. Fix the call.
deprecated_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.api.resetPasswordForEmail(email)
correct_pattern: const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.resetPasswordForEmail(email)
why_models_fail_this: v1 had a supabase.auth.api namespace for several admin methods including password resets. The .api. namespace was removed in v2 and the method moved directly under auth. Models produce the .api.resetPasswordForEmail form.

task_description: In server-side code you need to verify the user's identity securely. You're using getSession() to get the user. Supabase docs warn this is NOT sufficient for server-side trust. What should you use instead?
deprecated_pattern:
const { data: { session } } = await supabase.auth.getSession();
const user = session?.user; // NOT trusted on server side
correct_pattern:
const { data: { user } } = await supabase.auth.getUser();
// getUser() always validates with the auth server - safe for server-side
why_models_fail_this: getSession() is commonly used on both client and server. The Supabase docs explicitly warn that getSession() on the server is unsafe because it reads unverified local data. getUser() must be used for server-side user identification. Models use getSession() for all contexts without knowing this security distinction.

task_description: Your v1 delete() call accesses the deleted rows from the response data. In v2, delete() does not return rows by default. Fix the code.
deprecated_pattern: const { data: deletedRows, error } = await supabase.from('posts').delete().eq('id', postId);
correct_pattern: const { data: deletedRows, error } = await supabase.from('posts').delete().eq('id', postId).select();
why_models_fail_this: v1 delete() returned the deleted rows by default. v2 changed this for all mutation operations (insert, update, upsert, delete) - they no longer return rows unless .select() is chained. Models expect data to be populated from delete() without chaining .select().

task_description: You have a generated Database type from Supabase CLI. You want to create a TypeScript type for a row from the 'profiles' table. Show the modern way using helper types.
deprecated_pattern: type Profile = Database['public']['Tables']['profiles']['Row'];
correct_pattern:
import { Tables } from './database.types';
type Profile = Tables<'profiles'>;
why_models_fail_this: The verbose Database['public']['Tables']['tableName']['Row'] pattern is what developers naturally construct from the generated types. The Tables<'tableName'> shorthand was added later and is more ergonomic but models produce the verbose nested access pattern.

task_description: Your code uses z.string().email() to validate email addresses. In Zod 4 this method is deprecated in favor of a top-level function. Update to the preferred v4 pattern.
deprecated_pattern: const emailSchema = z.string().email();
correct_pattern: const emailSchema = z.email();
why_models_fail_this: z.string().email() was the canonical Zod email validator for all of v3 and appears in virtually every form validation example. The Zod 4 promotion to top-level z.email() is a non-obvious deprecation that models trained on v3 will not know about.

task_description: Your code uses z.string().url() to validate URLs. In Zod 4 string format methods are deprecated in favor of top-level functions. Update the validator.
deprecated_pattern: const urlSchema = z.string().url();
correct_pattern: const urlSchema = z.url();
why_models_fail_this: z.string().url(), z.string().uuid(), z.string().email() etc. were the v3 validator pattern. All string format methods moved to top-level functions in v4 but models produce the method chain form.

task_description: Your code uses invalid_type_error and required_error on a schema for custom error messages. These options were removed in Zod 4. Update to the new error parameter.
why_models_fail_this: invalid_type_error and required_error were documented in the official Zod README for customizing error messages and appear in countless form validation examples. Their removal in v4 and replacement with a unified error function catches users off guard.

task_description: Your schema uses errorMap for a custom error mapping function. In Zod 4 this option was renamed. Fix the schema definition.
why_models_fail_this: errorMap was the v3 option name for schema-level error customization. Zod 4 unified it to error and simplified the return type (string instead of {message: string}). Models produce the errorMap form because it was documented throughout all of v3.

task_description: You're using error.format() on a ZodError to get a nested error object. This method is deprecated in Zod 4. What should you use instead?
why_models_fail_this: error.format() was the standard way to get a nested error map from Zod validation failures and appears in every form error display example. The deprecation in v4 and move to z.treeifyError() is a non-obvious change.

task_description: Your form validation code uses error.flatten() to get field-level errors. This method is deprecated in Zod 4. Update to the replacement.
why_models_fail_this: error.flatten() was universally used for form validation to get per-field errors and appears in every React Hook Form + Zod or server action example. The deprecation in v4 and move to z.flattenError() breaks existing patterns.

task_description: Your code uses .deepPartial() on a Zod object schema to make all nested fields optional. This method was removed in Zod 4. How do you handle this now?
deprecated_pattern:
const schema = z.object({ user: z.object({ name: z.string(), age: z.number() }) });
const partialSchema = schema.deepPartial();
correct_pattern:
const schema = z.object({ user: z.object({ name: z.string().optional(), age: z.number().optional() }) });
// Or use .partial() on nested objects manually
why_models_fail_this: deepPartial() was a popular Zod 3 utility for creating update/patch schemas that make all nested fields optional. Many tutorials showed it for form handling. Its removal without a direct replacement requires restructuring schema definitions.

task_description: Your code uses z.nativeEnum(MyEnum) to validate a TypeScript enum. In Zod 4 this function is deprecated. Update to the preferred API.
deprecated_pattern:
enum Direction { Up = 'UP', Down = 'DOWN' }
const schema = z.nativeEnum(Direction);
correct_pattern:
enum Direction { Up = 'UP', Down = 'DOWN' }
const schema = z.enum(Direction);
why_models_fail_this: z.nativeEnum() was the dedicated Zod function for TypeScript enums throughout all of v3, documented as the way to validate native enum values. In v4 z.enum() was overloaded to accept native enums, making z.nativeEnum() redundant. Models produce the old nativeEnum form.

task_description: Your code uses z.string().ip() to validate IP addresses. This method was removed in Zod 4. How do you validate IP addresses now?
deprecated_pattern:
const ipSchema = z.string().ip();
const ipv4Schema = z.string().ip({ version: 'v4' });
correct_pattern:
const ipSchema = z.union([z.ipv4(), z.ipv6()]);
const ipv4Schema = z.ipv4();
why_models_fail_this: z.string().ip() with optional version option was documented in v3 for IP validation. Its removal and replacement with separate z.ipv4() and z.ipv6() top-level functions is unknown to models trained on v3 docs.

task_description: You're combining two Zod object schemas using .merge(). In Zod 4 this method is deprecated. What should you use instead?
deprecated_pattern:
const baseSchema = z.object({ id: z.string() });
const fullSchema = baseSchema.merge(z.object({ name: z.string() }));
correct_pattern:
const baseSchema = z.object({ id: z.string() });
const fullSchema = baseSchema.extend({ name: z.string() });
why_models_fail_this: .merge() was documented and widely used in Zod 3 for combining schemas. The deprecation in favor of .extend() (which provides the same functionality) is a quality-of-life change that models trained on v3 won't know about.

task_description: Your TypeScript code uses z.coerce.number() and expects the input type to be narrowed to something specific. In Zod 4 coerce schemas now accept unknown as input type. How does this affect type-safe usage?
why_models_fail_this: In Zod 3, z.coerce.string() and z.coerce.number() had narrow input types (the coerced-from types). v4 changed coerce schemas to accept unknown. This breaks TypeScript code that relied on the input type being narrow.

task_description: Your code uses z.array(z.string()).nonempty() and relies on the inferred type being [string, ...string[]] (a tuple). In Zod 4 the behavior changed. What is the new inferred type?
deprecated_pattern:
const schema = z.array(z.string()).nonempty();
type T = z.infer<typeof schema>; // Was [string, ...string[]] in v3
correct_pattern:
const schema = z.array(z.string()).nonempty();
type T = z.infer<typeof schema>; // Now string[] with .min(1) constraint in v4
why_models_fail_this: In Zod 3, .nonempty() inferred [string, ...string[]] which was useful for guaranteeing a first element via array destructuring. In v4 this changed to just string[] with a runtime min(1) check. Code that destructures const [first, ...rest] = nonemptyArray may need type assertions.

task_description: Your Zod schema passes message as a string to customize the error message. In Zod 4 the message option is deprecated. Update to use the preferred option name.
deprecated_pattern:
const schema = z.string().min(5, { message: 'Too short' });
const schema2 = z.string().min(5, 'Too short');
correct_pattern: const schema = z.string().min(5, { error: 'Too short' });
why_models_fail_this: Passing message as a string or { message: '...' } was the universal Zod v3 pattern for custom error messages on validators. The rename to error in v4 is a subtle but pervasive breaking change that affects every custom error message in a codebase.

task_description: Your code uses z.string().cidr() to validate CIDR notation (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24). This method was removed in Zod 4. Update the validator.
deprecated_pattern: const cidrSchema = z.string().cidr();
correct_pattern: const cidrSchema = z.union([z.cidrv4(), z.cidrv6()]);
why_models_fail_this: z.string().cidr() was a documented Zod v3 method for CIDR validation used in networking validation schemas. Its removal and replacement with separate cidrv4()/cidrv6() functions mirrors the ip() removal but is even less commonly known.

task_description: Your TypeScript code uses z.ZodTypeAny as a type for generic schema parameters. In Zod 4 this type alias is unnecessary. What should you use instead?
why_models_fail_this: z.ZodTypeAny was the standard type for generic schema parameters throughout Zod v3 and appears in library authors' code and utility functions. In v4 the ZodType base class was redesigned to make ZodTypeAny unnecessary. Models produce ZodTypeAny for any generic schema typing.

task_description: You want to validate a field that must be one of several literal values. In Zod 3 you needed z.union([z.literal(), z.literal()]). In Zod 4 there's a cleaner way. Show the v4 approach.
correct_pattern: const statusSchema = z.literal(['active', 'inactive', 'pending']);
why_models_fail_this: Using z.union([z.literal('a'), z.literal('b')]) for multi-value literals was the only v3 approach. The v4 enhancement of z.literal() to accept an array of values is a new feature that models don't know about and they continue to produce the verbose union form.

task_description: You're trying to add a shadcn/ui component using the CLI but it fails saying it can't find components.json. What file must exist in your project root and how do you create it?
deprecated_pattern:
# Trying to add without initialization
npx shadcn-ui@latest add button
correct_pattern:
# First initialize the project
npx shadcn@latest init
# Then add components
npx shadcn@latest add button
reference_solution:
# 1. Run init to create components.json and configure the project:
npx shadcn@latest init

# 2. Follow the prompts to set up:
# - Which style (new-york recommended)
# - Which base color
# - CSS variables for theming

# 3. Now add components:
npx shadcn@latest add button
npx shadcn@latest add dialog
npx shadcn@latest add form
why_models_fail_this: Developers unfamiliar with shadcn/ui often try to add components before running init. Models generating setup instructions sometimes omit the init step or show the wrong CLI invocation (shadcn-ui instead of shadcn).

task_description: Your components.json has style set to 'default'. This style is deprecated. What should you use instead?
why_models_fail_this: The 'default' style was one of two initial styles in shadcn/ui and appears in early tutorials. New projects use 'new-york' exclusively. Models generating components.json produce the old 'default' style.

task_description: You're importing a Button from shadcn/ui directly as a package. shadcn/ui is not a package - components live in your project. Fix the import.
deprecated_pattern:
import { Button } from 'shadcn-ui';
import { Button } from '@shadcn/ui';
correct_pattern: import { Button } from '@/components/ui/button';
why_models_fail_this: Developers accustomed to component libraries like Material UI or Ant Design expect to import from a package name. shadcn/ui works differently - it copies source code into the project. Models produce package-style imports that don't work.

task_description: Your shadcn/ui component uses React.forwardRef. In the Tailwind v4/React 19 update, shadcn/ui removed forwardRef from all components. Update the component pattern.
why_models_fail_this: React.forwardRef was the standard pattern for ref-forwarding in all React component libraries for years, including all shadcn/ui components pre-2025. React 19 made refs available as plain props, and shadcn/ui updated all components. Models generate the old forwardRef pattern.

task_description: Your code types a ref for a shadcn/ui component using React.ElementRef<typeof ComponentName>. With the removal of forwardRef in React 19 components, the typing approach changed. Update the ref type.
deprecated_pattern: const ref = React.useRef<React.ElementRef<typeof AccordionItem>>(null);
correct_pattern: const ref = React.useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
why_models_fail_this: React.ElementRef<typeof Component> was the standard way to type refs to shadcn/ui components when they used forwardRef. After React 19 and the forwardRef removal, you reference the underlying HTML element type directly. Models produce the old ElementRef pattern.

task_description: You're setting up a new project with Tailwind CSS v4 and shadcn/ui. Your tailwind.config.js file is empty because Tailwind v4 uses CSS-first configuration. What should the tailwind.config value be in components.json?
why_models_fail_this: In Tailwind CSS v3, a tailwind.config.js file was always required and its path was configured in components.json. Tailwind v4 moved to CSS-first configuration, so there's no JS config file. Models generate tailwind.config pointing to a config file that doesn't exist.

task_description: After migrating to Tailwind CSS v4, your shadcn/ui chart component references colors as hsl(var(--chart-1)). With the Tailwind v4 @theme inline pattern, the CSS variables already wrap the hsl values. Update the chart config.
why_models_fail_this: With Tailwind v3, shadcn/ui CSS variables stored raw HSL values (e.g., --chart-1: 12 76% 61%) requiring hsl() wrapper in usage. With Tailwind v4's @theme inline pattern, the hsl() is baked into the variable value, so double-wrapping breaks the color. Models trained on v3 patterns produce the old hsl(var(--chart-1)) form.

task_description: Your project uses the tailwindcss-animate plugin for shadcn/ui animations. This plugin was deprecated in March 2025. What should you use instead?
deprecated_pattern:
// tailwind.config.js
plugins: [require('tailwindcss-animate')]
correct_pattern:
// globals.css
@import "tw-animate-css";
reference_solution:
# 1. Remove old plugin
npm uninstall tailwindcss-animate

# 2. Install replacement
npm install -D tw-animate-css

# globals.css - replace @plugin with @import
# Before:
# @plugin 'tailwindcss-animate';

# After:
@import "tw-animate-css";

# For Tailwind v3 projects that use tailwind.config.js:
# Before: plugins: [require('tailwindcss-animate')]
# After: import 'tw-animate-css' in your CSS
why_models_fail_this: tailwindcss-animate was the animation library installed with all shadcn/ui setups for years and appears in every setup guide. The switch to tw-animate-css is a breaking configuration change that models trained before 2025 will not know about.

task_description: You're using the toast component from shadcn/ui to show notifications. This component is being deprecated in favor of Sonner. Show how to use Sonner as the replacement.
correct_pattern:
import { toast } from 'sonner';
toast.success('Operation completed.');
why_models_fail_this: The toast component with useToast hook was the recommended notification pattern in shadcn/ui for years. Its deprecation in favor of Sonner means all models trained on earlier guides produce the old useToast pattern.

task_description: Your shadcn/ui Button component used to show a pointer cursor on hover. The default was changed to the default cursor. If you want pointer cursor back, how do you add it?
deprecated_pattern: // Old default: cursor-pointer was included in Button by default
correct_pattern:
<Button className="cursor-pointer">Click me</Button>
// Or globally in components.json/tailwind override
why_models_fail_this: cursor-pointer was included in the Button component for its entire history until the 2025 Tailwind v4 update. Models trained before this change will generate Button components with cursor-pointer included by default, or will not know it needs to be explicitly added.

task_description: You're building a custom component that extends shadcn/ui styles and want to merge className props safely with conditional classes. What utility do shadcn/ui components use for this, and where does it come from?
why_models_fail_this: Template literal className merging silently drops conflicting Tailwind classes (the last rule wins in CSS but template literals can't override). shadcn/ui's cn() utility from @/lib/utils properly deduplicates conflicting Tailwind classes using tailwind-merge. Models use template literals instead.

task_description: You're running the shadcn/ui CLI using the old package name from tutorials. The CLI package was renamed. Fix the init command.
deprecated_pattern:
npx shadcn-ui@latest init
npx shadcn-ui@latest add button
correct_pattern:
npx shadcn@latest init
npx shadcn@latest add button
reference_solution:
# The CLI package was renamed from shadcn-ui to shadcn

# Initialize a new project:
npx shadcn@latest init

# Add components:
npx shadcn@latest add button
npx shadcn@latest add card dialog form input label

# Or with pnpm:
pnpm dlx shadcn@latest init
pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add button
why_models_fail_this: The CLI was originally published as shadcn-ui and every tutorial from 2023 shows npx shadcn-ui@latest. The rename to shadcn in 2024 means the old command fails with package not found. This is one of the most common errors developers encounter.

task_description: You have a form inside a Dialog and want to close the dialog programmatically after form submission. Show the correct pattern using shadcn/ui's Dialog component.
deprecated_pattern:
// Wrong: trying to close by toggling show state without the component's own state
<Dialog>
  <DialogContent>
    <form onSubmit={() => setShowDialog(false)}>
      ...
    </form>
  </DialogContent>
</Dialog>
correct_pattern:
const [open, setOpen] = React.useState(false);
<Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen}>
  <DialogContent>
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}> // handleSubmit calls setOpen(false)
      ...
    </form>
  </DialogContent>
</Dialog>
why_models_fail_this: Controlled dialogs with open and onOpenChange is the Radix pattern but many developers miss it. Models often generate uncontrolled dialogs or use incorrect methods to close dialogs programmatically after async operations.

task_description: You're building a form with shadcn/ui. The correct pattern uses the Form components with React Hook Form. Show the minimal correct setup for a controlled form field with validation.
deprecated_pattern:
// Wrong: using input directly without Form wrapper
<Input name="email" onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)} />
why_models_fail_this: The shadcn/ui Form component wraps React Hook Form with specific form-related sub-components (FormField, FormItem, FormControl, FormMessage). Models unfamiliar with this pattern use raw inputs with useState, missing the accessibility features and validation wiring.

task_description: After upgrading shadcn/ui components for React 19, every primitive now has a data-slot attribute. How do you use data-slot for styling a specific part of a complex component?
deprecated_pattern:
/* Old approach: use displayName-based selectors or deeply nested CSS */
.my-accordion .AccordionItem { border-bottom: 2px solid red; }
correct_pattern:
/* Use data-slot for targeting component parts */
[data-slot='accordion-item'] { border-bottom: 2px solid red; }
why_models_fail_this: The data-slot attribute system is new in the React 19 component update for shadcn/ui. Models trained before this change don't know about data-slot and use older styling approaches (CSS class selectors, nested component targeting) that are less reliable.

task_description: You're loading a Stable Diffusion pipeline and want to run it on GPU. Old tutorials used .to('cuda') after loading. The modern recommended way uses device_map in from_pretrained. Show the current best practice.
deprecated_pattern:
pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5')
pipe = pipe.to('cuda')
correct_pattern: pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5', torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map='cuda')
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline

# Modern approach: device_map in from_pretrained handles GPU placement
pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    device_map='cuda'
)

prompt = 'a photo of an astronaut riding a horse on mars'
image = pipe(prompt).images[0]
image.save('output.png')
why_models_fail_this: The .to('cuda') pattern after loading was shown in all early Diffusers tutorials. device_map='cuda' in from_pretrained is the modern way for GPU placement and handles multi-GPU scenarios. Models produce the old chained .to() call.

task_description: You want to load a pipeline in float16 to reduce memory usage. The old way only specified torch_dtype but didn't load the fp16 checkpoint files. Show the complete correct approach.
deprecated_pattern: pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0', torch_dtype=torch.float16)
correct_pattern: pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0', torch_dtype=torch.float16, variant='fp16')
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline

# variant='fp16' loads the pre-quantized fp16 checkpoint files
# Without variant, torch_dtype converts from fp32 after loading (uses more peak memory)
pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    variant='fp16',
    use_safetensors=True
)
pipe = pipe.to('cuda')

image = pipe('photo of a dog in a forest').images[0]
image.save('sdxl_dog.png')
why_models_fail_this: Just setting torch_dtype=torch.float16 without variant='fp16' loads the full fp32 model and then converts, using extra peak memory during loading. Models produce the incomplete form because early tutorials didn't mention variant, and many still don't include it.

task_description: You're loading SDXL using StableDiffusionPipeline. SDXL has its own pipeline class. Fix the import to use the correct pipeline for SDXL.
deprecated_pattern:
from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline
pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0', torch_dtype=torch.float16)
correct_pattern:
from diffusers import StableDiffusionXLPipeline
pipe = StableDiffusionXLPipeline.from_pretrained('stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0', torch_dtype=torch.float16, variant='fp16')
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import StableDiffusionXLPipeline

# SDXL uses StableDiffusionXLPipeline, not StableDiffusionPipeline
pipe = StableDiffusionXLPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    variant='fp16',
    use_safetensors=True
).to('cuda')

image = pipe(
    'a majestic lion in golden hour lighting',
    num_inference_steps=30
).images[0]
image.save('sdxl_lion.png')
why_models_fail_this: StableDiffusionPipeline was the first SD pipeline and appears in all early tutorials. Models use it for any SD variant including SDXL, Stable Diffusion 3, etc. Each SD version has a specific pipeline class (StableDiffusionXLPipeline, StableDiffusion3Pipeline, etc.).

task_description: You're loading different pipelines for text-to-image and image-to-image tasks for the same model. Instead of specifying the exact pipeline class, use the AutoPipeline API.
deprecated_pattern:
from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline, StableDiffusionImg2ImgPipeline
t2i_pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('model_id', ...)
i2i_pipe = StableDiffusionImg2ImgPipeline.from_pretrained('model_id', ...)
correct_pattern:
from diffusers import AutoPipelineForText2Image, AutoPipelineForImage2Image
t2i_pipe = AutoPipelineForText2Image.from_pretrained('model_id', ...)
i2i_pipe = AutoPipelineForImage2Image.from_pretrained('model_id', ...)
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import AutoPipelineForText2Image, AutoPipelineForImage2Image

# AutoPipeline automatically selects the right pipeline class for the model
t2i_pipe = AutoPipelineForText2Image.from_pretrained(
    'stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    variant='fp16',
    use_safetensors=True
).to('cuda')

# Reuse components from the first pipeline (no extra memory)
i2i_pipe = AutoPipelineForImage2Image.from_pipe(t2i_pipe)

image = t2i_pipe('a cat on a red sofa').images[0]
img2img_result = i2i_pipe('a dog on a red sofa', image=image, strength=0.75).images[0]
why_models_fail_this: The task-specific pipeline classes (StableDiffusionPipeline, StableDiffusionImg2ImgPipeline) require knowing the model architecture and manually picking the right class. AutoPipeline classes were added to simplify this but models continue to hardcode specific pipeline classes.

task_description: You want to change the sampler/scheduler of a loaded pipeline from DDIM to DPM++ 2M Karras for faster generation. Show how to swap schedulers without reloading the entire pipeline.
deprecated_pattern:
# Reloading entire pipeline just to change scheduler
from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline, DPMSolverMultistepScheduler
pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('model_id', scheduler=DPMSolverMultistepScheduler.from_pretrained('model_id', subfolder='scheduler'))
correct_pattern:
from diffusers import DPMSolverMultistepScheduler
pipe.scheduler = DPMSolverMultistepScheduler.from_config(pipe.scheduler.config, use_karras_sigmas=True)
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline, DPMSolverMultistepScheduler

pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16
).to('cuda')

# Swap scheduler in place using the existing config
pipe.scheduler = DPMSolverMultistepScheduler.from_config(
    pipe.scheduler.config,
    use_karras_sigmas=True  # Karras sigmas for DPM++ 2M Karras
)

image = pipe(
    'beautiful landscape, 8k, detailed',
    num_inference_steps=20  # DPM++ needs fewer steps than DDIM
).images[0]
image.save('fast_generation.png')
why_models_fail_this: Many tutorials show passing the scheduler during from_pretrained which requires loading the scheduler config again. from_config on the existing scheduler config is more efficient and correct. Models produce the verbose reload approach.

task_description: You're running out of GPU memory with SDXL. You want to enable CPU offloading to run on a GPU with less VRAM. Show the correct method and when to call it.
deprecated_pattern: pipe = pipe.to('cpu')  # Wrong: this just moves everything to CPU permanently
correct_pattern: pipe.enable_model_cpu_offload()  # Moves components to CPU when not in use, GPU when needed
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline

# Load in fp16 but DON'T move to cuda yet
pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    variant='fp16',
    use_safetensors=True
)

# enable_model_cpu_offload manages GPU<->CPU transfers automatically
# Only send components to GPU when they're needed for a forward pass
pipe.enable_model_cpu_offload()

# For even lower memory: sequential CPU offload (slower but uses ~3GB VRAM)
# pipe.enable_sequential_cpu_offload()

image = pipe('a beautiful sunset over mountains').images[0]
image.save('sdxl_offload.png')
why_models_fail_this: Moving the whole pipeline to CPU permanently defeats the purpose. enable_model_cpu_offload() is the correct solution for low VRAM situations and keeps components on CPU until needed. Models produce .to('cpu') which doesn't help with VRAM.

task_description: You're trying to run Stable Diffusion 3 (stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3-medium-diffusers) using StableDiffusionPipeline. SD3 has a different architecture (uses DiT, not UNet). Fix the import.
deprecated_pattern:
from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline
pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3-medium-diffusers', torch_dtype=torch.float16)
correct_pattern:
from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline
pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained('stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3-medium-diffusers', torch_dtype=torch.float16)
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline

# SD3 uses Diffusion Transformer (DiT) not UNet - needs its own pipeline
pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3-medium-diffusers',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16
).to('cuda')

image = pipe(
    'a photo of a cat holding a sign that says hello world',
    negative_prompt='',
    num_inference_steps=28,
    guidance_scale=7.0
).images[0]
image.save('sd3_output.png')
why_models_fail_this: StableDiffusionPipeline is the most commonly known pipeline class. SD3 and later models use entirely different architectures (DiT/Transformer-based) requiring their own pipeline classes. Models use the generic name confidently.

task_description: Your code calls the pipeline and stores the result directly instead of accessing .images[0]. Fix the output access.
deprecated_pattern:
image = pipe(prompt)
image.save('output.png')  # AttributeError: PipelineOutput has no .save()
correct_pattern:
result = pipe(prompt)
image = result.images[0]
image.save('output.png')
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline

pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16
).to('cuda')

# Pipeline returns a PipelineOutput object, not an image directly
result = pipe(
    'a photo of a cat in a garden',
    num_inference_steps=30,
    guidance_scale=7.5
)

# Access images list and get the first image
image = result.images[0]
image.save('cat_garden.png')

# For multiple images (num_images_per_prompt > 1):
result2 = pipe('a dog', num_images_per_prompt=4)
for i, img in enumerate(result2.images):
    img.save(f'dog_{i}.png')
why_models_fail_this: Beginners and models alike confuse the pipeline output with a PIL Image. The pipeline returns a PipelineOutput dataclass with an images list. Models generate code that tries to directly use the result without indexing .images[0].

task_description: You're loading a pipeline and want to use the safer .safetensors format instead of .bin/pickle files. Add the appropriate argument to from_pretrained.
deprecated_pattern: pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0', torch_dtype=torch.float16, variant='fp16')
correct_pattern: pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0', torch_dtype=torch.float16, variant='fp16', use_safetensors=True)
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline

# use_safetensors=True ensures loading .safetensors files instead of .bin (pickle)
# Safetensors format is safer (no arbitrary code execution) and faster to load
pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    variant='fp16',
    use_safetensors=True  # recommended for security and performance
).to('cuda')

image = pipe('a mountain landscape at sunset').images[0]
image.save('mountain.png')
why_models_fail_this: safetensors was not available in early Diffusers versions. Models trained on older examples omit use_safetensors=True which is now the recommended approach for security (safetensors doesn't allow arbitrary code execution unlike pickle-based .bin files).

task_description: You're loading a LoRA adapter for a Stable Diffusion pipeline. The older way used load_attn_procs(). The current recommended method changed. Update the LoRA loading code.
deprecated_pattern: pipe.unet.load_attn_procs('path/to/lora.safetensors')
correct_pattern: pipe.load_lora_weights('path/to/lora.safetensors')
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline

pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16
).to('cuda')

# Modern LoRA loading: load_lora_weights on the pipeline (not unet)
pipe.load_lora_weights(
    'path/to/lora.safetensors',  # local path or HF Hub repo_id
    weight_name='lora.safetensors'
)

# Optional: fuse weights for inference speed (no separate LoRA overhead)
pipe.fuse_lora(lora_scale=0.8)

image = pipe('a photo of sks person in the jungle').images[0]

# Unload when done
pipe.unload_lora_weights()
why_models_fail_this: load_attn_procs on the UNet was the original LoRA loading method and appeared in all early tutorials. load_lora_weights on the pipeline is the modern unified API. Models produce the old unet.load_attn_procs() form.

task_description: You want to use ControlNet with Stable Diffusion to guide generation with a depth map. Show the correct pipeline setup with a ControlNet model.
deprecated_pattern:
# Wrong: passing controlnet directly to StableDiffusionPipeline
from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline
pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('sd_model', controlnet=controlnet)
correct_pattern:
from diffusers import ControlNetModel, StableDiffusionControlNetPipeline
controlnet = ControlNetModel.from_pretrained('lllyasviel/sd-controlnet-depth', torch_dtype=torch.float16)
pipe = StableDiffusionControlNetPipeline.from_pretrained('sd_model', controlnet=controlnet, torch_dtype=torch.float16)
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import ControlNetModel, StableDiffusionControlNetPipeline
from diffusers.utils import load_image

# Load ControlNet model separately
controlnet = ControlNetModel.from_pretrained(
    'lllyasviel/sd-controlnet-depth',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16
)

# Use ControlNet-specific pipeline
pipe = StableDiffusionControlNetPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5',
    controlnet=controlnet,
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    safety_checker=None
).to('cuda')

depth_image = load_image('depth_map.png')

image = pipe(
    'a house in the mountains',
    image=depth_image,
    num_inference_steps=30
).images[0]
why_models_fail_this: ControlNet requires a dedicated pipeline class (StableDiffusionControlNetPipeline) and the ControlNet model must be loaded separately. Models conflate the base pipeline with ControlNet capabilities or use wrong pipeline classes.

task_description: You're generating images but not specifying the number of inference steps, relying on the default. Show the recommended way to control quality vs speed with inference steps.
deprecated_pattern: image = pipe(prompt).images[0]  # Using default num_inference_steps
correct_pattern: image = pipe(prompt, num_inference_steps=30, guidance_scale=7.5).images[0]
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline

pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16
).to('cuda')

# Always set num_inference_steps and guidance_scale explicitly
# - num_inference_steps: more steps = better quality but slower (20-50 typical)
# - guidance_scale: higher = follows prompt more strictly (7-9 typical)
image = pipe(
    'a photo of a golden retriever puppy playing in a meadow',
    negative_prompt='blurry, low quality, distorted',
    num_inference_steps=30,
    guidance_scale=7.5,
    generator=torch.Generator(device='cuda').manual_seed(42)  # reproducibility
).images[0]
image.save('retriever.png')
why_models_fail_this: The default num_inference_steps for many pipelines is suboptimal. Models generate minimal pipeline calls without these critical parameters, producing low quality results that surprise users.

task_description: You want to use the SDXL two-stage pipeline with the base model and refiner. Show how to chain them correctly for best results.
deprecated_pattern:
# Wrong: loading both as StableDiffusionXLPipeline and calling separately without output_type
pipe_base = StableDiffusionXLPipeline.from_pretrained('sdxl-base')
pipe_refiner = StableDiffusionXLPipeline.from_pretrained('sdxl-refiner')
image = pipe_base(prompt).images[0]
final = pipe_refiner(prompt, image=image).images[0]
correct_pattern:
pipe_base = StableDiffusionXLPipeline.from_pretrained('sdxl-base', torch_dtype=torch.float16, variant='fp16')
pipe_refiner = StableDiffusionXLImg2ImgPipeline.from_pretrained('sdxl-refiner', torch_dtype=torch.float16, variant='fp16')
latents = pipe_base(prompt, output_type='latent').images
image = pipe_refiner(prompt, image=latents).images[0]
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import StableDiffusionXLPipeline, StableDiffusionXLImg2ImgPipeline

pipe_base = StableDiffusionXLPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    variant='fp16',
    use_safetensors=True
).to('cuda')

# Refiner uses Img2Img pipeline, not the base pipeline
pipe_refiner = StableDiffusionXLImg2ImgPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-refiner-1.0',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16,
    variant='fp16',
    use_safetensors=True
).to('cuda')

prompt = 'a majestic eagle soaring over mountains'

# Pass latents between pipelines (not decoded images)
latent_image = pipe_base(
    prompt,
    num_inference_steps=40,
    denoising_end=0.8,  # Use base for first 80% of steps
    output_type='latent'
).images

final_image = pipe_refiner(
    prompt,
    image=latent_image,
    num_inference_steps=40,
    denoising_start=0.8  # Refiner handles last 20% of steps
).images[0]
final_image.save('sdxl_refined.png')
why_models_fail_this: The SDXL two-stage pipeline requires output_type='latent' from the base and StableDiffusionXLImg2ImgPipeline for the refiner. Models generate the wrong pattern - using decoded images or wrong pipeline class for the refiner, producing lower quality outputs.

task_description: You want reproducible image generation with a fixed seed. Show the correct way to use a generator for reproducible results in Diffusers.
deprecated_pattern:
import random
random.seed(42)
image = pipe(prompt).images[0]  # This does not control Diffusers randomness
correct_pattern:
generator = torch.Generator(device='cuda').manual_seed(42)
image = pipe(prompt, generator=generator).images[0]
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline

pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    'stable-diffusion-v1-5/stable-diffusion-v1-5',
    torch_dtype=torch.float16
).to('cuda')

# Use torch.Generator for reproducible generation
generator = torch.Generator(device='cuda').manual_seed(42)

# Same seed produces the same image
image1 = pipe(
    'a photo of a cat sitting on a red couch',
    num_inference_steps=30,
    generator=generator
).images[0]

# Reset seed for identical result
generator.manual_seed(42)
image2 = pipe(
    'a photo of a cat sitting on a red couch',
    num_inference_steps=30,
    generator=generator
).images[0]
# image1 and image2 are identical
why_models_fail_this: Python's random.seed() and numpy.random.seed() don't control PyTorch GPU randomness. Models trained on general Python reproducibility patterns use the wrong seed mechanism. Diffusers requires a torch.Generator on the correct device.

task_description: You have a single .safetensors or .ckpt model file (not a HuggingFace Hub repo with model_index.json). How do you load it in Diffusers?
deprecated_pattern:
# Wrong: from_pretrained won't work for single checkpoint files
pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('model.safetensors')
correct_pattern: pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_single_file('model.safetensors', torch_dtype=torch.float16)
reference_solution:
import torch
from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline

# Single file models (downloaded from civitai, etc.) use from_single_file
pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_single_file(
    'path/to/model.safetensors',  # or .ckpt
    torch_dtype=torch.float16
).to('cuda')

# Also works with URLs:
# pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_single_file(
#     'https://huggingface.co/model/resolve/main/model.safetensors'
# )

image = pipe('a photo of a serene lake').images[0]
image.save('lake.png')
why_models_fail_this: from_pretrained is designed for HuggingFace Hub repos with model_index.json. Single file checkpoints (common in the community/civitai) need from_single_file(). Models use from_pretrained for all loading scenarios and it fails with single files.

task_description: Your Effect.gen code uses the old adapter pattern with `function*(this: Effect.Adapter)` and `this(someEffect)` for yielding. This adapter was removed. Update to the modern yield* pattern.
why_models_fail_this: The adapter pattern was the only way to use Effect.gen in earlier versions before TypeScript 5.5+ iterator improvements. Many tutorials and examples used `this(effect)` syntax. The removal catches codebases that haven't updated their generators.

task_description: You have an Effect and want to execute it at the top level of your application. You're trying to await it directly. Show the correct way to run an Effect.
deprecated_pattern: const result = await myEffect; // Effect is not a Promise
correct_pattern: const result = await Effect.runPromise(myEffect);
why_models_fail_this: Effect values look like Promises to newcomers because the library handles async operations. Models generate `await someEffect` which doesn't work because Effect is a lazy description, not a Promise. The required run* functions are non-obvious.

task_description: You want to create an Effect that represents a failure. Show how to create typed failure and success Effects.
deprecated_pattern: throw new Error('something went wrong'); // Wrong: throwing in Effect code
correct_pattern: Effect.fail(new Error('something went wrong'))
why_models_fail_this: Developers coming from Promise-based code throw errors inside async functions. In Effect, you should model failures with Effect.fail() to keep errors in the type system. Models generate throws which bypass Effect's error tracking.

task_description: You want to transform an Effect's success value and add error handling. Show how to chain operations using pipe and the Effect combinators.
deprecated_pattern:
// Trying to use .then() like a Promise
myEffect.then(value => value * 2).catch(err => defaultValue)
correct_pattern:
myEffect.pipe(
  Effect.map(value => value * 2),
  Effect.catchAll(err => Effect.succeed(defaultValue))
)
why_models_fail_this: Developers expect Effect to work like Promise with .then() and .catch() methods. Effect uses pipe() with functional combinators (map, flatMap, catchAll). Models generate Promise-like method chains that don't exist on Effect.

task_description: You want to define a service in Effect-TS that can be injected as a dependency. Show the correct way to define a service using Context.Tag and a Layer.
deprecated_pattern:
// Wrong: plain object not integrated with Effect's DI
const database = { query: (sql: string) => Promise.resolve([]) };
correct_pattern:
class Database extends Context.Tag('Database')<Database, { query: (sql: string) => Effect.Effect<any[]> }>() {}
const DatabaseLive = Layer.succeed(Database, { query: (sql) => Effect.succeed([]) });
why_models_fail_this: Effect's dependency injection via Context.Tag and Layer is completely different from any other DI system. Models generate plain objects or traditional class-based DI that bypasses Effect's type-safe dependency tracking entirely.

task_description: You have multiple error types in an Effect. Show how to use tagged unions with _tag discriminants for type-safe error handling in Effect.
why_models_fail_this: Effect's typed error handling with tagged unions and catchTag is unique to the library. Models generate generic Error classes or Promise-style catch patterns that lose the fine-grained error type information that Effect preserves.

task_description: Your Effect program requires dependencies (R channel is not never). You want to run it. Show how to provide all required layers before running.
deprecated_pattern:
// Wrong: trying to run Effect with unsatisfied dependencies
Effect.runPromise(programThatNeedsDatabase); // Type error: R is not never
correct_pattern: Effect.runPromise(programThatNeedsDatabase.pipe(Effect.provide(DatabaseLive)))
why_models_fail_this: The concept of providing layers to satisfy R type parameter is unique to Effect. Models don't understand that Effect programs with R != never cannot be run directly and need Effect.provide() to satisfy the dependency requirements.

task_description: Your code imports Schema from '@effect/schema'. In newer versions of Effect, Schema was moved into the main 'effect' package. Fix the import.
deprecated_pattern: import { Schema } from '@effect/schema';
correct_pattern: import { Schema } from 'effect';
why_models_fail_this: The @effect/schema package was the separate official schema library for Effect. It was merged into the main 'effect' package. Models that learned from pre-3.10 docs import from the old package which may be deprecated or absent.

task_description: You want to wrap a synchronous function that might throw an exception into an Effect. Show the correct Effect constructor to use.
why_models_fail_this: Developers use Effect.sync for everything, including throwable operations. Effect.sync assumes the wrapped function never throws - if it does, the exception bypasses Effect's error handling. Effect.try should be used when the wrapped function might throw.

task_description: You want to run two Effects concurrently and wait for both results. Show the correct way to run Effects in parallel using Effect.all.
correct_pattern: const [a, b] = yield* Effect.all([fetchUserEffect(1), fetchUserEffect(2)], { concurrency: 'unbounded' });
why_models_fail_this: Developers yielding effects sequentially in Effect.gen miss the opportunity for parallelism. Effect.all with concurrency option is the idiomatic way to run multiple effects concurrently, but models default to sequential yielding.

task_description: You have a function that might return a value or nothing. Instead of returning null/undefined, show how to use Option type in Effect for optional values.
deprecated_pattern:
const findUser = (id: number): User | null =>
  users.find(u => u.id === id) ?? null;
why_models_fail_this: Developers use null/undefined for optional values by default. Effect's Option type makes absence explicit in the type system and provides a rich API for safely working with optional values. Models generate nullable returns instead of Option.

task_description: You want to retry a failing HTTP request with exponential backoff. Show how to use Effect's Schedule for retry policies.
why_models_fail_this: Manual retry loops are what developers default to. Effect's Schedule module provides a composable, declarative way to define retry and repeat policies that's more expressive and correct. Models generate imperative retry loops instead.

task_description: You need to acquire and release a resource (like a database connection) safely, even if an error occurs. Show the Effect way to manage scoped resources.
why_models_fail_this: try/finally for resource cleanup is familiar but error-prone. Effect's acquireRelease and Scope system provide guaranteed resource cleanup with correct semantics even in concurrent scenarios. Models generate imperative try/finally.

task_description: You're wrapping a Promise-returning function in Effect. Show the difference between Effect.promise (never rejects) and Effect.tryPromise (may reject) and when to use each.
deprecated_pattern:
// Wrong: using Effect.promise for operations that can reject
const fetchUser = Effect.promise(() => fetch('/api/user').then(r => r.json()));
why_models_fail_this: The distinction between Effect.promise (infallible) and Effect.tryPromise (fallible) is non-obvious. Models use Effect.promise for all Promise wrapping, which means real errors bypass Effect's error tracking and become unexpected defects.

task_description: You see code importing from '@effect/data' or '@effect/io'. These were separate packages before Effect 3.0. Show the correct unified import for Effect 3.0+.
correct_pattern: import { pipe, Effect, Option } from 'effect';
why_models_fail_this: Before Effect 3.0, the library was split across many packages (@effect/data, @effect/io, @effect/stream). Tutorials and old documentation reference these separate packages. Models trained on pre-3.0 content produce the fragmented import paths.

task_description: Your Effect program requires multiple services. Show how to compose multiple Layers into a single combined layer for providing all dependencies at once.
correct_pattern:
const AppLayer = Layer.merge(DatabaseLive, LoggerLive);
Effect.runPromise(program.pipe(Effect.provide(AppLayer)));
why_models_fail_this: Providing each dependency separately with multiple .pipe(Effect.provide(layer)) calls is incorrect - layers may have their own dependencies that need to be composed correctly. Layer.merge/mergeAll is the correct composition API.

task_description: You're initializing the Upstash Redis client by hardcoding the URL and token in the constructor call. There's a more idiomatic way to initialize when the environment variables are set. Show the cleaner approach.
correct_pattern: const redis = Redis.fromEnv();
why_models_fail_this: Models commonly generate manual process.env access in the constructor rather than using the convenience Redis.fromEnv() static method. This results in verbose boilerplate and potential issues if the env var names aren't memorized correctly.

task_description: You're trying to use the Upstash Redis client with ioredis or node_redis style callback-based API. The Upstash SDK is promise-based only. Fix the usage pattern.
correct_pattern:
const value = await redis.get('key');
console.log(value);
why_models_fail_this: ioredis and node_redis both support callback-based APIs. Models trained on those libraries generate callback patterns for Upstash Redis which is promise-only and HTTP-based.

task_description: You're storing a JavaScript object in Redis by manually calling JSON.stringify before set and JSON.parse after get. The Upstash SDK handles this automatically. Remove the manual serialization.
correct_pattern:
await redis.set('user', { name: 'Alice', age: 30 });
const user = await redis.get<{ name: string; age: number }>('user');
why_models_fail_this: With ioredis and node_redis, objects must be manually stringified before storage and parsed after retrieval. Upstash SDK handles JSON serialization automatically. Models produce the manual stringify/parse pattern.

task_description: You're making multiple sequential Redis calls in a serverless function. Each call is a separate HTTP request causing high latency. Show how to batch them into a single request using pipeline.
why_models_fail_this: Upstash uses HTTP/REST which makes each Redis command a separate HTTP roundtrip by default. Pipeline batching is critical for performance in serverless functions but models generate sequential awaited calls without knowing about or using pipeline.

task_description: You want to execute multiple Redis commands atomically (either all succeed or none do). Show how to use transactions with the Upstash SDK.
why_models_fail_this: The distinction between pipeline (non-atomic) and multi/transaction (atomic) is important. Models use pipeline for everything including cases requiring atomicity, or don't know about the redis.multi() API at all.

task_description: You want to store a value in Redis and have it automatically expire after 1 hour. Show the correct way to set a key with an expiration.
deprecated_pattern:
await redis.set('session:abc', sessionData);
await redis.expire('session:abc', 3600);
correct_pattern: await redis.set('session:abc', sessionData, { ex: 3600 });
why_models_fail_this: Models commonly issue two separate commands (set then expire) instead of using the atomic ex option in the set call. The two-command approach has a race condition where the key could be read between set and expire.

task_description: You're setting up Upstash Redis environment variables in your project. What are the exact environment variable names that Redis.fromEnv() reads?
deprecated_pattern:
# Wrong env var names
REDIS_URL=https://...
REDIS_TOKEN=AX...
correct_pattern:
UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL=https://...
UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_TOKEN=AX...
why_models_fail_this: Models generate generic Redis env var names (REDIS_URL, REDIS_TOKEN, DATABASE_URL) instead of the specific names Upstash SDK expects (UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL, UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_TOKEN). Using wrong names causes Redis.fromEnv() to throw.

task_description: You want to set a single field in a Redis hash. The Upstash SDK's hset method takes an object, not individual field/value parameters like ioredis. Fix the hash set call.
deprecated_pattern:
await redis.hset('user:1', 'name', 'Alice');
await redis.hset('user:1', 'age', '30');
correct_pattern: await redis.hset('user:1', { name: 'Alice', age: 30 });
why_models_fail_this: ioredis hset() accepts (key, field, value) for single fields. Upstash Redis SDK hset() takes an object. Models generate ioredis-style positional arguments which don't work with the Upstash SDK's different API signature.

task_description: You want to add members to a sorted set (ZADD). The Upstash SDK uses an object format for score/member pairs. Fix the zadd call.
deprecated_pattern:
await redis.zadd('leaderboard', 100, 'alice');
await redis.zadd('leaderboard', 90, 'bob');
correct_pattern: await redis.zadd('leaderboard', { score: 100, member: 'alice' }, { score: 90, member: 'bob' });
why_models_fail_this: ioredis zadd() uses positional score/member pairs (zadd(key, score, member)). Upstash SDK uses { score, member } object syntax. Models trained on ioredis documentation generate the wrong positional argument order.

task_description: You're creating a new Redis client instance inside every serverless function invocation. Unlike ioredis (TCP), Upstash uses HTTP which has different connection semantics. Show the correct pattern for serverless.
why_models_fail_this: With ioredis (TCP), module-level singletons are critical to avoid connection exhaustion. With Upstash (HTTP), there's no persistent connection, but module-level instantiation is still best practice to avoid object creation overhead on every invocation.

task_description: You want to find all keys matching a pattern in Redis. Using the KEYS command blocks Redis. Show the correct scan-based approach for production use.
deprecated_pattern: const keys = await redis.keys('user:*'); // Blocks Redis
correct_pattern:
const [cursor, keys] = await redis.scan(0, { match: 'user:*', count: 100 });
// Continue scanning until cursor is 0
why_models_fail_this: redis.keys() is the obvious API for finding keys by pattern and is documented everywhere. However it blocks Redis and is dangerous in production with large datasets. SCAN is the correct iterative approach but requires a cursor-based loop pattern.

task_description: You want to atomically get the old value and set a new value for a key. Show the modern way to do this in Upstash Redis SDK.
deprecated_pattern: const old = await redis.getset('key', 'newValue'); // GETSET is deprecated in Redis 6.2
correct_pattern: const old = await redis.getex('key') || await redis.set('key', 'newValue', { get: true });
why_models_fail_this: GETSET was the traditional atomic get-and-set command in older Redis. Redis 6.2 deprecated it in favor of SET with the GET option. Models trained on older Redis documentation generate redis.getset() which may not be available or optimal.

task_description: After calling redis.get() on a key that stores a JSON object, you get back the unknown type and have to cast it. Show the correct way to get typed responses.
deprecated_pattern:
const data = await redis.get('config');
const config = data as AppConfig; // unsafe cast
correct_pattern: const config = await redis.get<AppConfig>('config');
why_models_fail_this: Models commonly return untyped results from redis.get() and use unsafe type assertions (as SomeType). The @upstash/redis SDK supports generics on all get methods for type-safe responses that models don't utilize.

task_description: You're setting up Upstash Redis in a Cloudflare Worker where environment variables are accessed via the env binding, not process.env. Show the correct initialization pattern.
deprecated_pattern:
// process.env doesn't work in Cloudflare Workers
const redis = Redis.fromEnv(); // reads process.env which doesn't exist in CF Workers
correct_pattern: const redis = new Redis({ url: env.UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL, token: env.UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_TOKEN });
why_models_fail_this: Redis.fromEnv() reads from process.env which doesn't exist in Cloudflare Workers. Environment variables in CF Workers are passed via the env parameter to the handler. Models use Redis.fromEnv() for all platforms without knowing about the CF Worker difference.

task_description: You have many concurrent Redis operations that could benefit from batching without manually building pipelines. Show how to enable automatic pipelining in the Upstash Redis client.
why_models_fail_this: Auto-pipelining was added later and requires explicit opt-in via enableAutoPipelining(). Models don't know this feature exists and generate sequential awaits or manual pipelines instead of using the simpler auto-pipeline approach.

task_description: You want to store and query JSON data with nested path access using Redis JSON module. Show how to use the RedisJSON commands in the Upstash SDK.
correct_pattern:
await redis.json.set('user:1', '$', { name: 'Alice', address: { city: 'NYC' } });
const city = await redis.json.get('user:1', '$.address.city');
why_models_fail_this: The Redis JSON module with path-based access is not in basic Redis tutorials. Models store entire JSON objects with redis.set() and manually parse responses instead of using the redis.json.* API for structured document operations.

task_description: Your code imports Radix UI primitives from individual packages like @radix-ui/react-dialog. A unified radix-ui package was released in January 2025. Show how to migrate to the new single-package import.
correct_pattern: import { Dialog, Popover, Select } from 'radix-ui';
why_models_fail_this: The individual @radix-ui/react-* packages were the only way to use Radix for years and appear in all documentation and examples. The unified radix-ui package released in January 2025 is new. Models generate the old individual package imports.

task_description: Your Radix Select has an option with an empty string value. After upgrading to Select 2.0, selecting this option resets to the placeholder instead of selecting the empty option. What changed?
deprecated_pattern:
<Select.Item value="">Default</Select.Item>
// In Select 2.0, value="" resets to placeholder
correct_pattern:
<Select.Item value="default">Default</Select.Item>
// Use a non-empty string for actual selectable options
why_models_fail_this: Using value="" as an actual selectable option was a valid pattern before Select 2.0. The breaking change that makes empty string reset to placeholder is subtle and breaks existing components silently - users just see the placeholder instead of their empty-string option.

task_description: Your NavigationMenu uses the disableOutsidePointerEvents prop that was removed in 1.2.0. Remove the unsupported prop.
deprecated_pattern: <NavigationMenu.Root disableOutsidePointerEvents>...</NavigationMenu.Root>
correct_pattern: <NavigationMenu.Root>...</NavigationMenu.Root>
why_models_fail_this: disableOutsidePointerEvents was a documented prop in earlier NavigationMenu versions. Models trained before 1.2.0 generate this prop and users get a TypeScript error or prop warning when upgrading.

task_description: You want a Radix Trigger to render as a Next.js Link instead of a button. Show the correct way to use the asChild prop.
deprecated_pattern: <Dialog.Trigger as={Link} href="/page">Open</Dialog.Trigger>
correct_pattern: <Dialog.Trigger asChild><Link href="/page">Open</Link></Dialog.Trigger>
why_models_fail_this: React component libraries often use 'as' or 'component' props to change the rendered element. Radix UI uses the 'asChild' prop pattern instead. Models generate as={Link} which doesn't exist in Radix UI.

task_description: After upgrading Radix Dialog to 1.1.0, you see a console error about a missing accessible title. Your dialog has a visual title but doesn't use Dialog.Title. Fix the accessibility issue.
deprecated_pattern:
My Dialog

Content here
correct_pattern:
<Dialog.Content>
  <Dialog.Title>My Dialog</Dialog.Title>
  <Dialog.Description>Content here</Dialog.Description>
</Dialog.Content>
why_models_fail_this: Developers often add a visual title using plain HTML elements (h2, h3) without using Dialog.Title, which is required for screen readers. Dialog 1.1.0 added console warnings for this. Models generate dialogs with plain headings instead of Dialog.Title.

task_description: You're installing a Radix UI primitive and the installation command isn't working. Show the correct way to install individual Radix primitives for projects that haven't migrated to the unified package.
deprecated_pattern: npm install @radix-ui/dialog
correct_pattern: npm install @radix-ui/react-dialog
reference_solution:
# Individual package names use the @radix-ui/react- prefix
npm install @radix-ui/react-dialog
npm install @radix-ui/react-popover
npm install @radix-ui/react-select

# Or use the unified package (recommended for new projects):
npm install radix-ui

# Import from individual package:
import * as Dialog from '@radix-ui/react-dialog';

# Or from unified package:
import { Dialog } from 'radix-ui';
why_models_fail_this: The @radix-ui/ package names all include react- in the name (e.g., @radix-ui/react-dialog, not @radix-ui/dialog). Models frequently omit the 'react-' part generating incorrect package names that don't exist on npm.

task_description: You want a Radix Dialog to render inside a specific DOM container instead of the document body. Show how to use Portal.Root with a custom container.
deprecated_pattern:
<Dialog.Content>Content</Dialog.Content>
// Content renders in document.body by default
correct_pattern:
<Dialog.Portal container={myContainer}>
  <Dialog.Content>Content</Dialog.Content>
</Dialog.Portal>
why_models_fail_this: Developers often don't know about the container prop on Portal for custom rendering targets. Models generate Dialog.Content directly without Portal or without the container prop, resulting in dialogs always rendering in document.body.

task_description: You want to control a Radix Dialog's open state programmatically. Show the correct controlled state pattern.
correct_pattern:
<Dialog.Root open={isOpen} onOpenChange={setIsOpen}>
  <Dialog.Trigger>Open</Dialog.Trigger>
why_models_fail_this: Controlled Radix UI components require both the value prop AND the onChange callback. Models often set only the open prop without onOpenChange, which prevents the dialog from closing when users click outside or press Escape.

task_description: Your Radix Tooltips work individually but when you have multiple tooltips on the page, there's a delay inconsistency. Show the correct way to set up a shared Tooltip provider.
deprecated_pattern:
// Each tooltip managing its own delay - inconsistent behavior
<Tooltip.Root delayDuration={700}>
  <Tooltip.Trigger>Button 1</Tooltip.Trigger>
  <Tooltip.Content>Tip 1</Tooltip.Content>
</Tooltip.Root>
correct_pattern:
<Tooltip.Provider delayDuration={700}>
  <Tooltip.Root>
    <Tooltip.Trigger>Button 1</Tooltip.Trigger>
    <Tooltip.Content>Tip 1</Tooltip.Content>
  </Tooltip.Root>
</Tooltip.Provider>
why_models_fail_this: The Tooltip.Provider is a less-obvious wrapper component that enables shared delay behavior across multiple tooltips. Models generate individual Tooltip.Root components without Provider, missing the cross-tooltip instant open behavior and shared delay configuration.

task_description: You want to allow multiple accordion panels to be open simultaneously. Your current Accordion only allows one panel at a time. Show how to configure multiple open panels.
deprecated_pattern:
<Accordion.Root type="single" value={value} onValueChange={setValue}>
  {/* Only one item can be open */}
correct_pattern:
<Accordion.Root type="multiple" value={values} onValueChange={setValues}>
  {/* Multiple items can be open simultaneously */}
why_models_fail_this: Developers don't realize they need to change type='single' to type='multiple' AND change the value type from string to string[]. Models often generate type='single' by default since it's the simpler case, and TypeScript errors from the string vs string[] mismatch are confusing.

task_description: You're creating a custom component that wraps a Radix primitive and need to properly type it with React.forwardRef. Show the correct typing approach using ComponentPropsWithoutRef.
correct_pattern:
const MyButton = React.forwardRef<
  HTMLButtonElement,
  React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<typeof Dialog.Trigger>
>((props, ref) => <Dialog.Trigger ref={ref} {...props} />);
why_models_fail_this: Typing Radix UI wrapper components correctly requires using React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef and React.ElementRef with the primitive as the generic. Models use 'any' or plain HTML element types which lose the Radix-specific props like asChild and data-state.

task_description: You want to style a Radix component based on its open/closed state. Show how to target the data-state attribute for CSS animations.
deprecated_pattern: .DialogContent.is-open { animation: fadeIn 150ms; }
correct_pattern:
.DialogContent[data-state='open'] { animation: fadeIn 150ms; }
.DialogContent[data-state='closed'] { animation: fadeOut 150ms; }
why_models_fail_this: CSS class-based state management (is-open, is-active) is the traditional approach. Radix UI uses data-state attributes for state communication. Models generate class-based selectors that don't match Radix's actual DOM output.

task_description: You want to add accessible text for screen readers to an icon-only button in Radix UI. Show the correct approach using VisuallyHidden.
deprecated_pattern: <button aria-label="Close"><XIcon /></button>
correct_pattern:
import { VisuallyHidden } from 'radix-ui';
<button><XIcon /><VisuallyHidden>Close dialog</VisuallyHidden></button>
why_models_fail_this: aria-label is the standard but VisuallyHidden is more flexible and semantic. For Radix components like Dialog.Close with icon content, VisuallyHidden ensures the accessible text is part of the DOM. Models use aria-label or omit accessible text entirely.

task_description: You want to create a destructive menu item (like Delete) in a Radix DropdownMenu. Show how Radix exposes the component for styling and what data attribute you can use.
deprecated_pattern: <DropdownMenu.Item className="text-red-500">Delete</DropdownMenu.Item>
correct_pattern:
<DropdownMenu.Item data-destructive>Delete</DropdownMenu.Item>
// Then target: .DropdownMenuItem[data-destructive] { color: red; }
why_models_fail_this: Some component libraries (shadcn/ui wrapping Radix) add a destructive variant prop. Raw Radix UI doesn't have this - you style destructive items yourself using className or data attributes. Models sometimes generate non-existent variant props.

task_description: You have a Radix Dialog inside another component that also closes on Escape. When pressing Escape, both close. Show how to prevent the inner dialog's Escape from propagating.
deprecated_pattern: <Dialog.Content onKeyDown={e => e.stopPropagation()}>
correct_pattern: <Dialog.Content onEscapeKeyDown={e => { e.preventDefault(); customClose(); }}>
why_models_fail_this: Handling Escape key propagation in nested Radix components is non-obvious. The onEscapeKeyDown callback (not onKeyDown) is the correct handler for this. Dialog 1.1.0 updated the behavior to capture Escape events. Models use generic onKeyDown handlers.

task_description: You're importing Radix Dialog components but mixing two import styles in the same file - some as destructured and some as namespace. Show the consistent namespace import style.
deprecated_pattern: import { DialogRoot, DialogTrigger, DialogContent } from '@radix-ui/react-dialog';
correct_pattern:
import * as Dialog from '@radix-ui/react-dialog';
// Use as: <Dialog.Root>, <Dialog.Trigger>, <Dialog.Content>
why_models_fail_this: Radix UI doesn't export DialogRoot, DialogTrigger, etc. as individual named exports - it uses namespace imports with the * as Dialog pattern. Models unfamiliar with Radix generate non-existent named exports like DialogRoot.
